sections.title: May and might: possibility
sections.content:
May and might often have a similar meaning when we talk about possibility. However, we prefer may in academic or formal language to talk about characteristics or behaviour:
• The seeds from the plant may grow up to 20 centimetres in length.
and in speech we prefer might to say what we will possibly do in the future.
We can use may well (or less commonly, might well) to emphasise that something is unexpected:
• Keith may well pass the entrance examination after all. (or Keith might well…)

sections.title: May not used for questions about possibility
sections.content:
We don't use may to ask questions about the possibility of something happening. Instead we use, for example, could(n't) or the phrase be likely:
• Could it be that you don't want to leave? (not May it be that you …?)
• Are you likely to be in Spain again this summer? (not May you be in Spain …?)
It is possible to use might in this type of question, but it is rather formal:
• Might they be persuaded to change their minds?
Note that we can use may to ask for permission and offer help in a formal way:
• May I leave now?     May I help you?

sections.title: Might (not may) + bare infinitive for past typical situations
sections.content:
Might (not 'may') + bare infinitive is sometimes used to talk about what was typically the case in the past. This is a formal or literary use:
• During the war, the police might arrest you for criticising the government.
• Years ago, children might be sent down mines at the age of six. (passive form)
We can also use could + bare infinitive in examples like this to talk about past ability (see Unit 15). For example, 'During the war, the police could arrest you …' means that the police were legally able to arrest you.

sections.title: May/might not … but: compensating for a limitation
sections.content:
When we say that a person or thing compensates to some extent for a limitation or weakness by having another characteristic, we can use a pattern with may / might not + bare infinitive … but … or may / might not have + past participle … but …:
• The painting may not be a masterpiece, but the colours are remarkable.
• She might not have danced very gracefully, but she had a lot of energy and enthusiasm.

sections.title: May/might have + past participle; may/might be + -ing
sections.content:
We use may / might (not 'can') + have + past participle and may / might (not 'can') + be + -ing to talk about possible events in the past, present and future:
• Do you think Laura may / might have completed the report by now? (past)
• His maths may / might have improved by the time the exam comes round. (future)
• Marco isn't in his office. He may / might be working at home today. (present)
• When I go to Vienna I may / might be staying with Max, but I'm not sure yet. (future)
Note that could can be used in these sentences instead of may or might:
• Do you think Laura could have completed the report by now?
We can use may / might have been + -ing to talk about possible situations or activities that went on over a period of past time:
• Callum didn't know where the ball was, but he thought his sister might have been playing with it before she left for school.

exercises.question: We ___ go to Majorca for our holiday this summer.
exercises.hint: Informal speech about future possibility → might preferred.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: might (informal speech about future plans)
Informal speech about future possibility → might preferred.

exercises.question: The planet Venus ___ be seen clearly in the night sky this month.
___ you see Yasemin this weekend?
exercises.hint: Don't use 'may' for questions about possibility — use could or might.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both might and could possible
Don't use 'may' for questions about possibility — use could or might.

exercises.question: I feel really sore after playing tennis. I think I ___ have a bath.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: might (informal speech about future action)
Informal future possibility → might preferred.

exercises.question: Someone's left their coat. B: ___ it be Nadia's?
exercises.hint: Questions about possibility — might or could, not may.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both might and could work
Questions about possibility — might or could, not may.

exercises.question: Exceeding the stated dose ___ cause drowsiness.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: may (formal/instructional warning — characteristic)
Formal instruction/label context → may.

exercises.question: It ___ well be the case that the evidence has been tampered with.
acceptable: Both may well and might well possible
exercises.hint: 'May well' emphasises unexpectedness; 'might well' also possible.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both may well and might well possible
'May well' emphasises unexpectedness; 'might well' also possible.

exercises.question: You should have come dancing. You might have enjoyed / might enjoy it.
options: might have enjoyed (past possibility — didn't happen)
exercises.hint: Referring to a past event that didn't happen → might have enjoyed.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: might have enjoyed (past possibility — didn't happen)
Referring to a past event that didn't happen → might have enjoyed. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: She might have tried / might have been trying to get a book off the top shelf when she fell.
options: might have been trying (activity in progress when she fell)
exercises.hint: Emphasising the ongoing activity at the time → might have been trying.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: might have been trying (activity in progress when she fell)
We use the present perfect continuous here to emphasise an ongoing or recently continuing activity.
💡 Emphasising the ongoing activity at the time → might have been trying.

exercises.question: Dr Carter might have come / might be coming over this evening, so can you tidy the house?
options: might be coming (future possibility — present continuous)
exercises.hint: Future possibility → might be coming (present continuous form).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: might be coming (future possibility — present continuous)
Future possibility → might be coming (present continuous form).

exercises.sentence: She might to arrive late — the traffic is terrible.
exercises.correction: She might arrive late — the traffic is terrible.
exercises.hint: Modal verbs (may, might, can, could, will, would, shall, should, must) are followed directly by the base infinitive — never 'to'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: She might arrive late
All modal verbs are followed by the bare infinitive (without 'to'). 'Might to arrive' is never correct. This applies to all modals: might, may, can, could, will, would, shall, should, must.

exercises.sentence: May you help me carry these bags?
exercises.correction: Could you help me carry these bags?
acceptable: Would you help me carry these bags?
Can you help me carry these bags?
exercises.hint: 'May' is not used for requests in modern English — use 'could', 'would', or 'can'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Could/Would you help me...
'May' is used for permission ('May I leave?') and possibility ('It may rain'). For requests in modern English, 'Could you...?' or 'Would you...?' are standard. 'May you...?' for requests sounds archaic and unnatural.

exercises.sentence: It's possible that she might not comes to the party.
exercises.correction: It's possible that she might not come to the party.
exercises.hint: After 'might', always use the bare infinitive — no -s or -ing ending.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: she might not come
The verb after a modal (might, may, etc.) is always the bare infinitive — no third-person -s, no -ing, no -ed. The phrase 'it's possible that' is redundant when used with 'might' (both express possibility), but it is not grammatically wrong.

exercises.prompt: Rearrange to express possibility in the past:
exercises.hint: Subject + might + have + past participle = past possibility
exercises.explanation:
Answer: She might have already left
'Might have + past participle' expresses possibility about a past event. The adverb 'already' goes between 'have' and the past participle. Structure: subject + might + have + (adverb) + past participle.
